title: Collage & Craft
strapline: Feathers, foil and fabric — choosing slowly, snipping carefully, sticking with pride.
intent: Discriminate between textures and materials by handling them: bumpy, silky, crinkly, stiff — and find the words for the difference
Compose before committing: arranging, rearranging and only then sticking — or leaving it transient on purpose
Grow scissor skills across honest resistances — tissue gives easily, card fights back, fabric needs both hands thinking
Master glue as a genuine skill: how much, where, and whether this material needs glue at all or a bit of tape
Sort and select with intent — colour families, same-and-different, the exact right button
Value found and reclaimed materials: treasures from our own walks becoming art
implementation: Present materials in sorted, open trays — buttons here, fabric there, foil, natural bits — never one jumbled tub; choosing well needs seeing well
Offer a "try it first" arrangement tray or empty frame so composition can happen before any glue appears
Teach glue technique deliberately — spreading thinly, dots for small pieces — and let children pump, spread and manage it themselves
Grade the cutting on purpose: paper strips for snippers, drawn lines on card next, fabric for the experienced
Feed texture vocabulary as children handle materials: scrunchy, smooth, stiff, silky, rough
Bring treasures back from local walks into the collage trays, so children see their own finds become art
Ask how a piece was made, not just what it is, and display work with the child's own words
key_questions: How does that one feel — scrunchy or smooth?
Which piece will you lay down first?
Do you think glue will hold that, or does it need tape?
Have you tried it in a different place before you stick it?
Which of these go together, do you think — and why those?

impact.text: Our youngest crafters explore glue, paper and textures with enthusiasm and their own agenda — the sticking is the point, not the picture.
Children snip into paper strips and tissue with growing control — every snip is finger-strength in the bank.
Children spread glue, thread and place pieces using one-handed tools with growing control.
Children sort and match materials as they choose — building colour families, pairing near-identical buttons, spotting same and different.
Choices become deliberate: this fabric not that foil, scissors not tearing — and children mix materials just to see what happens. The finished piece is theirs, and they own it proudly.
Experienced makers cut card and fabric with precision and patience, and use spreaders, punches and scissors with real intent.
Children describe their collages with new texture words — crinkly, silky, stiff — and notice detail in friends' work.
Treasures collected on local walks — leaves, seed pods, blossom — reappear in collage, and children tell you what they found and where.

enhancements: A texture feely-bag of collage materials — find the silky one without looking
Sewing with plastic needles and hessian, or hole-punched cards and laces, for the next-level threaders
A season tray refreshed from walks: crunchy leaves in autumn, blossom and petals in spring
Weaving frames — a garden trellis threaded with fabric strips and ribbons over weeks
Foil, cellophane and a light box or sunny window for a shine-and-see-through collage
Family-photo collage invitations so craft connects to home
A transient-art table with frames and NO glue — some compositions are for today only, and a photo keeps them

playing_exploring: Open trays of materials invite handling, comparing and combining before any plan exists
Children play with texture and shine for its own sake — the investigating is the learning
active_learning: Cutting fabric, threading a lace and getting the glue amount right all reward another careful try
creating_thinking: Composing a collage is a chain of real decisions — first this, then that, moved twice, stuck once
Children develop their own ways of joining and arranging, and carry them from one make to the next
